title: Rightsizing & Waste Reduction
summary: Matching provisioned resources to actual usage, and finding the waste — idle, orphaned, mis-tiered — that accumulates by default in any growing fleet.

slides.markdown:
**Rightsizing** matches provisioned resources to actual usage — the highest-leverage cost lever most teams under-invest in, because it's invisible day-to-day and only shows up as savings on next month's bill.

- Waste isn't one villain — it's compute sized for a peak that rarely happens, storage nobody moved off the expensive tier, and resources orphaned after their VM was deleted.
- Rightsizing is **ongoing**, not a one-time cleanup — usage patterns drift.

Most fleets are sized once, for a guessed peak, and never revisited. Rightsizing means comparing an instance's actual CPU and memory utilization — typically from 2-4 weeks of monitoring data — against what it's provisioned for, and downsizing (or upsizing) to match.

A common finding: an instance averaging 8% CPU on a `4xlarge` costs the same whether it's doing real work or idling. Moving it to a size with real headroom over actual peaks cuts that line item roughly in proportion, with no user-visible change.

Not all data deserves the same storage tier. **Hot** storage (fast, expensive) suits data accessed constantly; **cool** and **cold/archive** tiers cost a fraction as much but add retrieval latency or fees.

Tiering means moving data to the cheapest tier that still meets its access pattern: logs older than 30 days, completed order records, or rarely-viewed media seldom need hot-tier speed. Years of untouched data left on hot storage is one of the most common, and most fixable, sources of storage overspend.

Some waste isn't oversized — it's **abandoned**. Common culprits: an unattached disk left behind after its VM was deleted, a load balancer still running with zero healthy targets, a forgotten snapshot kept "just in case" for years, or a dev environment nobody remembered to shut down.

None of these serve any workload, so none show up in a performance dashboard — only in the bill. Regular audits, or automated cleanup policies, are the only reliable way to catch them.

slides.sectionTitle: Choosing instance types by workload shape
slides.markdown:
| Workload shape | What it needs | Wrong choice looks like |
|---|---|---|
| CPU-bound | High vCPU-to-memory ratio | A memory-optimized instance running hot on CPU |
| Memory-bound | High memory-to-vCPU ratio | A compute-optimized instance swapping or OOM-killing |
| I/O-bound | High network/disk throughput, not raw CPU | A general-purpose instance bottlenecked on disk IOPS |

**How to decide:** profile the actual bottleneck — CPU, memory, or I/O wait — before picking a family. Matching family to bottleneck, not just total core count, is where most savings live.

slides.subTitle: A rightsizing pass with no performance loss
slides.markdown:
A team profiles its fleet: web-tier instances average 70% CPU (correctly sized), but the batch tier averages 12% CPU on memory-optimized instances doing CPU-heavy compression.

Switching the batch tier to compute-optimized instances at half the size **cuts that tier's cost by more than half** while jobs finish just as fast — because the new instances match the workload's actual bottleneck instead of over-provisioning memory nobody used.

slides.subTitle: Rightsizing once and never revisiting
slides.markdown:
The wrong belief: rightsizing is a project you do once and check off. Traffic patterns, feature usage, and data volumes all drift — a fleet rightsized for last year's load is quietly wrong again within months, sometimes now too *small*, not just too big.

The correct model: rightsizing is a recurring review — monthly or quarterly — often automated with recommendations from the provider's own cost tools, not a one-time cleanup sprint.
